guide.title: Chinatown, San Francisco: the Dragon Gate, Waverly Place and the alleys
guide.intro: San Francisco's Chinatown runs between Broadway and Bush Street, on ground that climbs steeply to the west. SF Planning describes it as some 350 buildings along Stockton Street, Grant Avenue, Kearny Street and the connecting side streets and alleys, and gives its period of significance as 1906 to 1930. Almost everything standing went up in the decade after the earthquake and fire of April 1906. Grant Avenue, called Dupont Street until the rebuilding, runs north through the quarter as 都板街, Du Pon Gai; Stockton Street is where the produce and the fish are sold. The alleys between them carry temples on their top floors and family association halls behind their balconies. One thing to know before you come: Portsmouth Square is closed for renovation through mid-2028.

sections.heading: The streets and the alleys
sections.body:
Chinatown is built to a grid of long blocks and short alleys, and almost all of it went up at once. SF Planning's parcel records bear that out frontage by frontage along Grant Avenue: 700-720 in 1906, 733-741 in 1906, 715-717 in 1907, 824-843 in 1908, 900-916 in 1908, 942-951 in 1907, and 1019-1029 in 1924. Waverly Place is the same story a block over, with Nos. 100-108, 143-147 and 151-155 dating from 1906 and Nos. 29-35 and 125-129 from 1911. SF Planning records the Chinatown Historic District as eligible for the National Register of Historic Places and for the California Register, and its own note on the record says that neither has been formalised officially.

Grant Avenue is the wide street, 都板街 in Chinese. Stockton Street, which SF Planning dates in the same years — 1000-1032 in 1907, 843 in 1908, 1009-1011 in 1910, 830-848 in 1915, 1040-1044 in 1920 — is where the produce and fish shops are. The alleys are where the temples and the association halls sit: Waverly Place, whose Chinese name 天后廟街 means Tin How Temple Street, after the temple on the top floor at No. 125; Ross Alley, laid out in 1849; Spofford Street, whose buildings SF Planning dates to 1906, 1907 and 1908. At Grant Avenue and California Street the Sing Chong Building faces the Sing Fat Building across the intersection. At 743 Washington Street is the building that housed the Chinese Telephone Exchange, which SF Planning dates to 1909.

Two institutions with long histories are working buildings rather than visitor sites, and a traveller reads them from the pavement. Gordon J. Lau Elementary School at 950 Clay Street opened in September 1859 as a segregated public school for Chinese children, later became the Oriental Public School, and was renamed in 1998 for the San Francisco supervisor Gordon J. Lau; a California law of 1860 barred "Negroes, Mongolians, and Indians" from the public schools and permitted segregated schools instead. Chinese Hospital at 845 Jackson Street traces its origins to 1899 and the Oriental Dispensary, which opened as the Tung Wah Yi Kuk at 828 Sacramento Street and moved after 1906 to 14 Trenton Street. Bruce Lee was born at Chinese Hospital on 27 November 1940.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
Chinatown-Rose Pak station is under Stockton Street at Washington Street and opened on 19 November 2022 as part of the Central Subway. Muni routes 1, 8, 30 and 45, the 8AX and 8BX peak expresses, the T Bus and the 91 Owl also serve it. The station structure extends 100 feet below ground and carries a 5,400-square-foot plaza on its roof.

The California Street cable car line crosses Grant Avenue. Stockton Street runs under the hill through the Stockton Street Tunnel, whose south portal is at Bush Street and whose north portal is at Sacramento Street; it opened in 1914 and holds a maximum grade of 4.29 percent, against the 18 percent climb north from Sutter Street and the 12 percent climb south from Sacramento Street that it replaced.

Steer by addresses. The Dragon Gate stands at Grant Avenue and Bush Street. Old St Mary's is at 660 California Street, on the corner of Grant Avenue. The Chinese Historical Society of America is at 965 Clay Street, the Chinatown/Him Mark Lai branch library at 1135 Powell Street and Donaldina Cameron House at 920 Sacramento Street. The Chinese Culture Center's Art Center and Design Store is at 667 Grant Avenue and its office at 750 Kearny Street, third floor mezzanine. Portsmouth Square is bounded by Kearny Street, Washington Street, Clay Street and Walter U. Lum Place. Willie "Woo Woo" Wong Playground is at 830 Sacramento Street, between Waverly Place and Pagoda Place, on the number given by Rec & Park's own project page and by OpenStreetMap; Rec & Park's property dataset gives 850 Sacramento Street for the same park.

sections.heading: What is open and what is shut
sections.body:
Start with the closure at the centre of the quarter. Rec & Park's advisory reads: "Portsmouth Square is now closed for renovation through mid-2028." Construction began on 10 June 2026, and demolition of the pedestrian bridge that carried walkers over Kearny Street was completed on 14 August 2026.

Four institutions publish their own hours. The Chinese Historical Society of America opens Wednesday and Saturday, 10am to 5pm, and states that it is closed on Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, Friday and Sunday; it names no admission price. The Chinatown/Him Mark Lai branch library opens Sunday 1 to 5, Monday 10 to 6, Tuesday to Thursday 10 to 8, Friday 1 to 6 and Saturday 10 to 6. The Chinese Culture Center's Art Center and Design Store opens 11am to 6pm, Thursday to Monday, its office 9am to 6pm, and its Him Mark Lai Learning Center by appointment. Old St Mary's gives church hours of Tuesday to Friday 10am to 4.30pm, Saturday 11.30am to 6pm and Sunday 8am to 3pm, with mass at 5pm on Saturday, 9am and 11am on Sunday and 12.05pm Tuesday to Friday.

The temples are harder. No source states opening hours for Tin How Temple, for Kong Chow Temple or for the Ma-Tsu Temple of U.S.A., so none are given here; photography is not permitted inside Tin How. The Golden Gate Fortune Cookie Factory's own site states two different sets of opening hours, so none are given for it either.

Among the places to eat and shop, Mister Jiu's, R&G Lounge, Z & Y Restaurant, Sam Wo, the Wok Shop and Red Blossom Tea Company all publish a full week on their own sites; Sam Wo opens Tuesday to Sunday, 11am to 9pm, and closes on Monday. Hang Ah Tea Room publishes only the current day's hours, so none are given here.

faq.question: Can you go into Portsmouth Square?
faq.answer: No. Rec & Park's advisory reads "Portsmouth Square is now closed for renovation through mid-2028." Construction began on 10 June 2026 and Swinerton Builders is the contractor; demolition of the pedestrian bridge over Kearny Street was completed on 14 August 2026. The rebuilt square is to have a flexible outdoor event space with an elevated stage, an 8,500-square-foot community clubhouse with an assembly area and meeting rooms, a shade structure, and a consolidated playground with adult fitness equipment. Rec & Park records the plaza as platted in about 1835 for the Yerba Buena settlement and renamed after the USS Portsmouth in 1846. Captain John Berrien Montgomery landed with seventeen men and raised the flag near the custom house on 9 July 1846, Sam Brannan announced the discovery of gold on 11 May 1848, and the square held a refugee camp after the earthquake and fire of 1906.

faq.question: Which buildings in Chinatown carry a designation?
faq.answer: Old St Mary's at 660 California Street is San Francisco Landmark No. 2, designated in 1968. Donaldina Cameron House at 920 Sacramento Street is San Francisco Landmark No. 44, designated in 1971. The Chinese Historical Society of America's building at 965 Clay Street is San Francisco Landmark No. 122, the Clay Street Center, designated in 1981. The branch library at 1135 Powell Street is San Francisco Landmark No. 235, the Chinatown Branch Carnegie Library, designated in 2002. The Chinatown Historic District itself is recorded by SF Planning as eligible for the National Register of Historic Places and for the California Register, and formalised in neither.

faq.question: Can you go into the temples?
faq.answer: Tin How Temple occupies the top floor of a building at 125 Waverly Place and is dedicated to the sea goddess Mazu, known in Cantonese as Tin How; photography is not permitted inside. Kong Chow Temple stands on Stockton Street above the post office and is dedicated to Guan Di, and the prediction slip Bess Truman drew on a visit in 1948 is displayed in it. The Ma-Tsu Temple of U.S.A. is at 30 Beckett Street. No source states opening hours for any of the three, so none are given here. Old St Mary's, a working Catholic parish, does publish hours: Tuesday to Friday 10am to 4.30pm, Saturday 11.30am to 6pm and Sunday 8am to 3pm.

faq.question: Where can you eat, and when?
faq.answer: Mister Jiu's, at 28 Waverly Place, opens Tuesday to Thursday 5pm to 9pm and Friday and Saturday 5pm to 9.30pm, closed Sunday and Monday, and takes reservations online only. R&G Lounge, at 631 Kearny Street, opens Sunday to Thursday 11am to 9pm and Friday and Saturday 11am to 9.30pm. Z & Y Restaurant, at 655 Jackson Street, opens 11.30am to 3pm and 4.30pm to 9pm on Monday and Wednesday to Sunday, and closes on Tuesday. Sam Wo, at 713 Clay Street, opens Tuesday to Sunday 11am to 9pm and closes on Monday. Hang Ah Tea Room at 1 Pagoda Place publishes only the current day's hours, so none are given here, and no source states hours for Great Eastern Restaurant, House of Nanking, Good Mong Kok Bakery, Eastern Bakery or Li Po Cocktail Lounge.

faq.question: What is the fortune cookie factory, and can you photograph it?
faq.answer: The Golden Gate Fortune Cookie Factory is at 56 Ross Alley, its main entrance on the alley between Jackson Street and Washington Street. Its own site says it makes up to 10,000 fortune cookies a day, baked fresh on a cast-iron rotating griddle wheel, and sells chocolate, strawberry and green-tea cookies as well as custom fortunes for collection in the shop. That same site gives two different sets of opening hours in two blocks on one page, so none are given here. Wikipedia records a charge of fifty cents for photographs of the workers and of the factory interior.

places.name: Dragon Gate
places.summary: A three-portal pailou facing south across Bush Street at the foot of Grant Avenue. A design competition sponsored by Mayor John F. Shelley in 1967, open to architects of Chinese descent, was won by the architect Clayton Lee with the landscape architects Melvin H. Lee and Joseph Yee. The central portal carries the inscription 天下為公, tianxia wei gong, attributed to Sun Yat-sen; the east portal carries 忠孝仁愛.
places.history: Wikipedia's account, which is footnoted to contemporary press, records groundbreaking in October 1967 and construction beginning in August 1968; that the 120 ochre roof tiles, the roofing and the guardian lions were fabricated and donated by the Republic of China in 1969; that the construction contract went to Moreau Construction and was completed at $90,889.15; and that the gate was dedicated on 18 October 1970, with a half-mile parade attended by Mayor Joseph Alioto and Vice-President Yen Chia-kan. It was restored in 1995, when the roof tiles were replaced, the lighting upgraded, the steps repaired and handrails installed. A male guardian lion stands at the west portal with his right fore paw on a pearl and a female at the east with her left fore paw on a cub; fish and dragons run along the roof, with a ball between the dragons.

places.name: Grant Avenue
places.summary: Grant Avenue runs north through Chinatown as 都板街, Du Pon Gai. It was called Dupont Street until the rebuilding that followed 1906, when it was renamed for President Ulysses S. Grant. Between Sutter and Geary two blocks were converted to two-way running in 2012 while Stockton Street was closed for Central Subway construction.
places.history: SF Planning's parcel records date the street frontage to the rebuilding: 700-720 Grant Avenue to 1906, 715-717 to 1907, 733-741 to 1906, 824-843 to 1908, 900-916 to 1908, 942-951 to 1907 and 1019-1029 to 1924.

places.name: Stockton Street
places.summary: Stockton Street is Chinatown's produce and fish market street, lined with three- and four-storey buildings with shops at street level and flats above.
places.history: SF Planning dates the street's buildings to the same rebuilding as Grant Avenue: 1000-1032 Stockton Street to 1907, 901-907 to 1907, 843 to 1908, 1009-1011 to 1910, 830-848 to 1915 and 1040-1044 to 1920. The Chinatown-Rose Pak station of the Central Subway runs beneath the street at Washington Street, and the Stockton Street Tunnel carries the roadway under the hill between Sacramento Street and Bush Street.

places.name: Waverly Place
places.summary: One block of Waverly Place runs between Sacramento Street and Washington Street, parallel to Grant Avenue and west of it. Its Chinese name is 天后廟街, Tianhou miao jie, Tin How Temple Street, after the temple on the top floor at No. 125; the street was called Pike Street before. Mister Jiu's is at No. 28, the First Chinese Baptist Church at No. 15 and the Bing Kong Tong Benevolent Association at No. 35.

places.name: Ross Alley
places.summary: Ross Alley, 舊呂宋巷, runs north and south for one block between Jackson Street and Washington Street, between Stockton Street and Grant Avenue. The Golden Gate Fortune Cookie Factory is at No. 56.
places.history: Wikipedia records that the alley was laid out in 1849 beside the house of the merchant Charles L. Ross, from whom the name comes, and that it was formerly Stout's Alley, for Dr Arthur Breese Stout, who bought that house. Iron doors on the alley's gambling establishments were banned by city ordinance in 1889. SF Planning dates Nos. 8-14 to 1906, Nos. 20 and 22-24 to 1907, No. 35 to 1910 and Nos. 41-53 to 1908.

places.name: Stockton Street Tunnel
places.summary: The tunnel carries Stockton Street under the hill, with its south portal at Bush Street and its north portal at Sacramento Street. It opened in 1914 and was built primarily for the streetcars of the F Stockton line.
places.history: Wikipedia records that a petition for the tunnel was filed on 23 January 1909. It was cut to ease the climb: the grade north from Sutter Street had been 18 percent and the grade south from Sacramento Street 12 percent, while the tunnel holds a maximum of 4.29 percent between Sacramento and Sutter. Stockton Street was lowered at the southern approach, which shows at 417 Stockton Street, where the basement became the ground floor and the old front door is a marked window bay on the second floor.

places.name: Tin How Temple
places.summary: Tin How Temple occupies the top floor of a building at 125 Waverly Place and is dedicated to the sea goddess Mazu, known in Cantonese as Tin How. The Sue Hing Benevolent Association, which had acquired the temple before the 1906 fire, put up the present four-storey building on the site and reopened the temple in 1910; SF Planning records the building's construction year as 1911. The temple closed in 1955 and reopened on 4 May 1975. Photography is not permitted inside. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Wikipedia records that the temple was destroyed in the fire of 1906, and that the image of the goddess, the temple bell and part of the altar survived it.

places.name: Kong Chow Temple
places.summary: Kong Chow Temple stands on Stockton Street above the post office and is dedicated to Guan Di. The association behind it was founded in 1849 and took the name Kong Chow Clan Association in 1854. The temple was destroyed in 1906 and rebuilt on its original Pine Street site; the present building dates from 1977. A prediction slip drawn by Bess Truman on a visit in 1948 is displayed inside.
places.history: Wikipedia records that the Pine Street building was demolished and the temple moved to the Stockton Street building it occupies now.

places.name: Ma-Tsu Temple of U.S.A.
places.summary: The Ma-Tsu Temple of U.S.A., 媽祖廟, is at 30 Beckett Street and is dedicated to Mazu. SF Planning records the construction year of 26-30 Beckett Street as 1908. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Wikipedia and Wikidata record that the temple was founded in 1986, with foundational ties to the Chaotian Temple in Beigang, Yunlin, in Taiwan, and that it moved from Grant Avenue to Beckett Street in 1996.

places.name: Old St Mary's Cathedral
places.summary: Old St Mary's stands at 660 California Street, on the corner of Grant Avenue. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 2, designated in 1968, and the site is also California Historical Landmark No. 810, listed on 30 December 1965. The parish gives church hours of Tuesday to Friday 10am to 4.30pm, Saturday 11.30am to 6pm and Sunday 8am to 3pm, with mass at 5pm on Saturday, 9am and 11am on Sunday and 12.05pm Tuesday to Friday. The telephone number is (415) 288-3800.
places.history: The cornerstone was laid on 17 July 1853 by Bishop Joseph S. Alemany, at what were then California and Dupont Streets, and the church was dedicated at midnight mass on Christmas 1854. It is Gothic Revival, designed by William Craine and Thomas England, and was built by Chinese labourers with brick brought round Cape Horn and granite cut in China. It served as the cathedral of the Archdiocese of San Francisco from 1854 until 1891 and has been a parish church ever since. The 1906 earthquake left it standing and the fire the next day gutted it: the exterior brick walls and the bell tower remained, and the bells and the marble altar melted. Under the clock face runs the inscription "Son, observe the time and fly from evil."

places.name: Buddha's Universal Church
places.summary: Buddha's Universal Church is a Buddhist church at 720 Washington Street. SF Planning records the building's construction year as 1964.
places.history: No source states an institutional history of the church, so none is given here.

places.name: First Chinese Baptist Church of San Francisco
places.summary: The First Chinese Baptist Church of San Francisco stands at 15 Waverly Place, at the Sacramento Street end of the block. SF Planning records the construction year of 1-15 Waverly Place as 1908.
places.history: Wikipedia records that the congregation was founded in 1880 by the missionary J. B. Hartwell as a Southern Baptist mission in a rented storefront, and that a permanent church under the Home Mission Board was established in 1888 at Waverly Place and Sacramento Street. The congregation broke away with thirteen others over Mayor Isaac Kalloch's anti-Chinese politics and became Northern Baptist. The building burned in the fire that followed the 1906 earthquake, and the congregation moved to Oakland while it was rebuilt.

places.name: Chinese Historical Society of America Museum and Learning Center
places.summary: The society's museum is at 965 Clay Street, in a building that is San Francisco Landmark No. 122, the Clay Street Center, designated in 1981. Its own site gives opening hours of Wednesday and Saturday, 10am to 5pm, and states that it is closed on Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, Friday and Sunday. No admission price is stated. The telephone number is 415 391 1188, extension 109.
places.history: The building was the Chinatown YWCA, designed by Julia Morgan. The San Francisco YWCA resolved in October 1929 to build on three lots bounded by Joice, Clay and Powell Streets; Morgan was contracted and, after consulting Chinese Americans, worked elements of Chinese arts and crafts into the design. SF Planning records the construction year as 1932. The building housed the YWCA until it was damaged in the Loma Prieta earthquake of 1989, and the YWCA board agreed to sell it to the society in 1996; the museum opened in the building in November 2001. The society itself was incorporated on 5 January 1963 and had earlier homes at 17 Adler Place from 1966 and at 650 Commercial Street from June 1989. Twelve Gum Shan paintings by Jake Lee and James Leong's mural One Hundred Years: History of the Chinese in America are on permanent display. The building is nicknamed the Lantern on the Hill.

places.name: Chinese Culture Center of San Francisco
places.summary: The centre's Art Center and Design Store is at 667 Grant Avenue and opens 11am to 6pm, Thursday to Monday. Its office is at 750 Kearny Street, third floor mezzanine, San Francisco, CA 94108, open 9am to 6pm, on (415) 986-1822 extension 025. The Him Mark Lai Learning Center, at 750 Kearny Street on the third floor, is by appointment only.
places.history: Wikipedia records that the centre is a non-profit established in 1965 as the operations centre of the Chinese Culture Foundation, which incorporated on 15 October 1965; that its facilities inside the hotel building at 750 Kearny Street run to 20,000 square feet and include a 299-seat auditorium, a 2,935-square-foot gallery, a gallery shop, a classroom and offices; that work on those facilities began on 27 January 1973; and that the space is leased at a nominal cost after lobbying by the local Chinese American community. Jenny Leung has been executive director since 2020, following Mabel Teng from 2009 to 2019.

places.name: Chinatown/Him Mark Lai Branch Library
places.summary: The branch's full official name is Chinatown/Him Mark Lai. San Francisco Public Library gives its hours as Sunday 1 to 5, Monday 10 to 6, Tuesday to Thursday 10 to 8, Friday 1 to 6 and Saturday 10 to 6, and its telephone number as 415-355-2888. The building is San Francisco Landmark No. 235, the Chinatown Branch Carnegie Library, designated in 2002.
places.history: SF Planning records the construction year as 1921. San Francisco Public Library describes the branch's holdings as including an extensive file of pamphlets, newspapers and magazine articles on Chinatown's history and on issues of concern to the Chinese and Asian American community. Rene Yung's Take Root, nine copper panels and lamps made in 1996, is set into the facade.

places.name: Donaldina Cameron House
places.summary: Cameron House stands at 920 Sacramento Street and is San Francisco Landmark No. 44, designated in 1971. SF Planning records the construction year as 1908. It is a working social service organisation, which describes its purpose on its own site as empowering the San Francisco Chinese community to build strength and resilience through family-centred programmes.
places.history: The building was formerly the Occidental Board Presbyterian Mission House and the Chinese Presbyterian Mission House. Wikipedia records that the Presbyterian Women's Occidental Board of Foreign Missions was organised by five women in 1873, and that the Mission House was formed in Chinatown in 1876 under Margaret Culbertson, first in a wooden building across the street at 933 Sacramento Street, as a home for Chinese girls escaping abusive employment or prostitution. Donaldina Cameron joined in 1895 and later directed the house. The adjoining parcel at 901-945 Sacramento Street carries a separate building of 1982.

places.name: Great Star Theater
places.summary: The Great Star Theater, 大星劇院, is at 636 Jackson Street; the telephone number is 415 735-4159. Its own site describes it as the Home of the Cantonese Opera. Wikipedia gives its capacity as 410 seats.
places.history: SF Planning records the construction year of 626-636 Jackson Street as 1925. It was built as the Great China Theater for Chinese opera. The Pacific Chinese Dramatic Club took offices in the theatre in 1930. Bruce Lee's father performed on its stage, and Lee himself appeared as an infant in the 1941 Cantonese film Golden Gate Girl, directed by Esther Eng. The theatre was refurbished from 2010 and reopened on 18 June 2021 by Alice Chu and Roger Pincombe.

places.name: Chinese Consolidated Benevolent Association
places.summary: The Chinese Consolidated Benevolent Association, 中華會館, known in English as the Chinese Six Companies, has its hall at 843 Stockton Street. SF Planning records the construction year as 1908.
places.history: Wikipedia records that the association was organised in the 1850s and formally established in 1882, and that the immigrants it served came mainly from eight districts on the west side of the Pearl River Delta in Guangdong.

places.name: Chinese American Citizens Alliance
places.summary: The national headquarters of the Chinese American Citizens Alliance is at 1044 Stockton Street. SF Planning records the construction year of 1040-1044 Stockton Street as 1920, which fits the completion of the headquarters building in the early 1920s.
places.history: Wikipedia records that the organisation was founded in San Francisco in 1895 as the Native Sons of the Golden State and renamed the Chinese American Citizens Alliance in 1915; that lodges were chartered in Los Angeles in 1914, San Francisco in 1915 and Oakland in 1917; and that it has twenty local lodges.

places.name: Bing Kong Tong Benevolent Association
places.summary: The Bing Kong Tong Benevolent Association, 秉公堂, has its hall at 35 Waverly Place; the telephone number is 415 982-2551. SF Planning records the construction year of 29-35 Waverly Place as 1911.
places.history: No source states a history of the association, so none is given here.

places.name: Chinese Telephone Exchange building
places.summary: The building at 743 Washington Street housed the Chinese Telephone Exchange. SF Planning records its construction year as 1909.
places.history: No source states a further history of the building, so none is given here.

places.name: Far East Cafe
places.summary: Far East Cafe is a restaurant on Grant Avenue, occupying Nos. 631 to 645. SF Planning records the construction year of 631-645 Grant Avenue as 1908.
places.history: No source states a history of the restaurant, so none is given here.

places.name: Portsmouth Square
places.summary: Portsmouth Square, 花園角, is bounded by Kearny Street on the east, Washington Street on the north, Clay Street on the south and Walter U. Lum Place on the west, and covers 1.484 acres, or 64,627 square feet. Rec & Park's own advisory reads: "Portsmouth Square is now closed for renovation through mid-2028." Construction began on 10 June 2026 and the contractor is Swinerton Builders. Demolition of the pedestrian bridge over Kearny Street was completed on 14 August 2026. The rebuilt square is to carry a flexible outdoor event space with an elevated stage, an 8,500-square-foot community clubhouse with an assembly area and meeting rooms, a shade structure, and a consolidated playground with adult fitness equipment.
places.history: Rec & Park records that the plaza was platted in about 1835 for the Yerba Buena settlement and renamed after the USS Portsmouth in 1846. Captain John Berrien Montgomery landed with seventeen men and raised the flag near the custom house on 9 July 1846; Sam Brannan announced the discovery of gold on 11 May 1848; and the square held a refugee camp after the earthquake and fire of 1906. Rec & Park states that the park is eligible for the California Register of Historic Resources for its role as an important cultural space for the Chinatown community. Walter U. Lum Place forms the square's western boundary.

places.name: Willie "Woo Woo" Wong Playground
places.summary: The playground is at 830 Sacramento Street, between Waverly Place and Pagoda Place, on a terraced hillside site of 0.656 acres, or 28,591 square feet. It has two sand-floor playgrounds, tennis and volleyball courts, and a clubhouse with a rooftop basketball court. At the park's western edge, Hang Ah Alley lies wholly within the park boundary. Rec & Park's project page and OpenStreetMap give the address as 830 Sacramento Street; Rec & Park's property dataset gives 850.
places.history: The park is named for the Chinese American basketball player Willie "Woo Woo" Wong, who played for the University of San Francisco. It was rebuilt on a budget of $14.5 million from the 2012 Clean and Safe Neighborhood Parks Bond and the Downtown Parks Fund, and opened to the public in February 2021. The site it stands on, 828 Sacramento Street, is where the Tung Wah Yi Kuk, the ancestor of Chinese Hospital, opened in 1899.

places.name: Chinatown-Rose Pak station
places.summary: An underground Muni Metro station beneath Stockton Street at Washington Street, opened on 19 November 2022 as part of the Central Subway and named for Rose Pak, the Chinatown political activist who helped secure support and funding for the station and for the T Third Street extension. It was designed by Kwan Henmi, now DLR Group. The structure extends 100 feet below ground and carries a 5,400-square-foot public plaza on its roof. Muni routes 1, 8, 30 and 45, the 8AX and 8BX peak expresses, the T Bus and the 91 Owl also serve it.
places.history: The building at 933-949 Stockton Street, which housed 56 low-income residents, was acquired by eminent domain and demolished for the station; the residents were relocated to a new building at Broadway and Sansome Street, with $8 million from the SFMTA among other grants. Stockton Street stayed open throughout construction from 2013, while a half-block of Washington Street was closed. A couplet by Carin Mui, 黃立慈, winner of a 2016 Chinatown Community Development Center contest, is printed in calligraphy on red opaque glass at the station plaza: 昔日漂洋採金礦，今朝劈地鋳銀龍 — "In the past we traveled across the Pacific to mine for gold; Now, we break through earth to form a silver dragon."

places.name: Mister Jiu's
places.summary: Mister Jiu's is at 28 Waverly Place. Its own site gives hours of Tuesday to Thursday 5pm to 9pm and Friday and Saturday 5pm to 9.30pm, closed Sunday and Monday, and states that it cannot take reservations by telephone or email, only through its reservations page.
places.history: The restaurant floor takes seated dinners, and the upstairs room, the Moongate Lounge, takes seated dinners and standing receptions.

places.name: R&G Lounge
places.summary: R&G Lounge is a Cantonese restaurant at 631 Kearny Street; the telephone number is 415 982-7877. Its own site gives hours of Sunday to Thursday 11am to 9pm and Friday and Saturday 11am to 9.30pm.
places.history: SF Planning records the construction year of 630-632 Kearny Street as 1908 and of 631-633 Kearny Street as 1910.

places.name: Z & Y Restaurant
places.summary: Z & Y Restaurant serves Szechuan food at 655 Jackson Street; the telephone number is 1 (415) 981-8988. Its own site gives hours of 11.30am to 3pm and 4.30pm to 9pm on Monday and Wednesday to Sunday, closed on Tuesday, and states that reservations are taken for parties of four or more at least a day in advance.
places.history: SF Planning records the construction year of 655-657 Jackson Street as 1907.

places.name: Great Eastern Restaurant
places.summary: Great Eastern Restaurant is at 649 Jackson Street. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: SF Planning records the construction year of 647-649 Jackson Street as 1908.

places.name: House of Nanking
places.summary: House of Nanking is at 919 Kearny Street; its own site gives the telephone number as (415) 421-1429. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the restaurant, so none is given here.

places.name: Hang Ah Tea Room
places.summary: Hang Ah Tea Room serves Cantonese dim sum at 1 Pagoda Place; the telephone number is 415 982-5686. Its own site publishes only the current day's hours rather than a weekly schedule, so no opening hours are given here.
places.history: SF Planning records the construction year of 1 Pagoda Place as 1911.

places.name: Sam Wo
places.summary: Sam Wo, 三和粥粉麵, is at 713 Clay Street. Its own site gives hours of Tuesday to Sunday, 11am to 9pm, and states that it is closed on Monday.
places.history: SF Planning records the construction year of 713-721 Clay Street as 1912. Wikipedia records that the earlier restaurant at 813 Washington Street closed in 2012 for safety reasons, that the business reopened on Clay Street in 2015, and that it closed briefly in 2025 and reopened the same year under new management. Edsel Ford Fung, who died in 1984, worked there in the 1960s, and some of the signs he wrote for the Washington Street room survive.

places.name: Good Mong Kok Bakery
places.summary: Good Mong Kok Bakery sells dim sum and Chinese pastries to take away, at 1039 Stockton Street; the telephone number is 415 397 2688. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the bakery, so none is given here.

places.name: Eastern Bakery
places.summary: Eastern Bakery, 東亞餅食公司, is at 720 Grant Avenue. Its side entrance on Commercial Street is Sullivan's Grotto, at 776 Commercial Street, which was a location in the 1950 film Woman on the Run, directed by Norman Foster. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: SF Planning records the construction year of 700-720 Grant Avenue as 1906.

places.name: Li Po Cocktail Lounge
places.summary: Li Po Cocktail Lounge is a bar at 916 Grant Avenue; the telephone number is 415 982-0072. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: SF Planning records the construction year of 900-916 Grant Avenue as 1908.

places.name: Golden Gate Fortune Cookie Factory
places.summary: The factory, 金門餅食公司, is at 56 Ross Alley, its main entrance on the alley between Jackson Street and Washington Street. The telephone number is 415 781-3956 and custom orders are on 415 806-8243. Its own site states that up to 10,000 fortune cookies are made a day, baked fresh on a cast-iron rotating griddle wheel, and that it sells chocolate, strawberry and green-tea cookies as well as custom fortunes for collection in the shop. The factory's own site states two different sets of opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Wikipedia records a charge of fifty cents for photographs of the workers and of the factory interior.

places.name: The Wok Shop
places.summary: The Wok Shop sells woks and Asian kitchenware at 718 Grant Avenue, between Sacramento Street and Clay Street. Its own site gives hours of 11am to 5pm, seven days a week, and the telephone number as 415-989-3797.
places.history: SF Planning records the construction year of 700-720 Grant Avenue as 1906.

places.name: Chinatown Kite Shop
places.summary: The Chinatown Kite Shop is at 717 Grant Avenue. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.

places.name: Red Blossom Tea Company
places.summary: Red Blossom Tea Company is at 831 Grant Avenue; the telephone number is (415) 395-0868. Its own site gives showroom hours of 11 to 5 on Monday and Wednesday to Friday and 10 to 5 on Saturday and Sunday, closed on Tuesday.
places.history: SF Planning records the construction year of 829-843 Grant Avenue as 1908.

places.name: Ping Yuen
places.summary: Ping Yuen, 平園, is a public housing complex of four buildings along Pacific Avenue with 434 apartments in all: West, Central and East Ping Yuen on the south side of the street, and North Ping Yuen. It is occupied housing and there is no visitor access.
places.history: Wikipedia records that the formal effort to build it began in 1939, that West, Central and East Ping Yuen were dedicated in 1951, and that North Ping Yuen followed in 1961. Each apartment had its own bathroom and kitchen from 1951, unlike the single-room-occupancy housing typical of the quarter. The murder of Julia Wong in 1978 prompted a residents' rent strike over maintenance and security, led by the future mayor Ed Lee. Ownership passed from the city to the Chinatown Community Development Center in 2016.

places.name: International Hotel Manilatown Center
places.summary: The building at 868 Kearny Street holds senior housing together with St Mary's School and the Manilatown Center. It opened in 2005, on the site of the International Hotel.
places.history: Wikipedia records that the International Hotel was established as a hotel for travellers in 1854, moved to Kearny Street in 1873 and was rebuilt in 1907 after the earthquake and fire of the previous year; that it had become a low-income single-room-occupancy hotel housing a largely Filipino American community; and that from about 1954 its basement held Enrico Banducci's original hungry i. All its tenants were evicted on 4 August 1977 and the building was demolished in 1981. The site was bought by International Hotel Senior Housing Inc. and rebuilt.

places.name: Sing Chong Building
places.summary: The Sing Chong Building stands at 616 Grant Avenue on the corner of California Street, facing the Sing Fat Building across the intersection.
places.history: No source states a construction date or a further history for the building, so none is given here.

entries.name: Dragon Gate
entries.note: A three-portal pailou at Grant Avenue and Bush Street, won in a 1967 design competition by Clayton Lee and dedicated on 18 October 1970.

entries.name: Grant Avenue
entries.note: Dupont Street until the rebuilding that followed 1906, and 都板街, Du Pon Gai, in Chinese; SF Planning dates its frontages to 1906, 1907, 1908 and 1924.

entries.name: Waverly Place
entries.note: One block between Sacramento and Washington Streets, its Chinese name meaning Tin How Temple Street, with the temple on the top floor at No. 125.

entries.name: Ross Alley
entries.note: Laid out in 1849 beside the merchant Charles L. Ross's house, formerly Stout's Alley, and now the address of the fortune cookie factory at No. 56.

entries.name: Portsmouth Square
entries.note: Closed for renovation through mid-2028; the plaza was platted in about 1835 and renamed after the USS Portsmouth in 1846.

entries.name: Old St Mary's Cathedral
entries.note: San Francisco Landmark No. 2, designated in 1968; the cornerstone was laid on 17 July 1853 and the church dedicated at midnight mass on Christmas 1854.

entries.name: Tin How Temple
entries.note: On the top floor at 125 Waverly Place, dedicated to the sea goddess Mazu; it closed in 1955, reopened on 4 May 1975, and permits no photography inside.

entries.name: Chinese Historical Society of America Museum and Learning Center
entries.note: In Julia Morgan's Chinatown YWCA of 1932 at 965 Clay Street, San Francisco Landmark No. 122, designated in 1981; open Wednesday and Saturday, 10am to 5pm.

entries.name: Chinatown/Him Mark Lai Branch Library
entries.note: San Francisco Landmark No. 235, the Chinatown Branch Carnegie Library, designated in 2002; SF Planning dates the building to 1921.

entries.name: Great Star Theater
entries.note: Built in 1925 as the Great China Theater for Chinese opera; refurbished from 2010 and reopened on 18 June 2021.

entries.name: Mister Jiu's
entries.note: At 28 Waverly Place, open Tuesday to Thursday 5pm to 9pm and Friday and Saturday 5pm to 9.30pm, with reservations taken online only.

entries.name: R&G Lounge
entries.note: Cantonese cooking at 631 Kearny Street, open Sunday to Thursday 11am to 9pm and Friday and Saturday 11am to 9.30pm.

entries.name: Golden Gate Fortune Cookie Factory
entries.note: Up to 10,000 cookies a day on a cast-iron rotating griddle wheel at 56 Ross Alley; photographs of the workers are charged at fifty cents.

entries.name: The Wok Shop
entries.note: Woks and Asian kitchenware at 718 Grant Avenue, between Sacramento and Clay Streets, open 11am to 5pm seven days a week.
